newsitem.title: ZAIRE: War threatens Zaire's free-market reforms.
newsitem.headline: War threatens Zaire's free-market reforms.

text.p: War in east Zaire, where rebels hold key towns near Rwanda and Burundi, is threatening free-market economic reforms designed to restore stability and boost foreign investment in this sprawling mineral-rich nation.

"We are in a very fragile position and could easily come off the rails. We have to maintain what we have achieved, (the war) could affect management of the economy in a very large way," Luboya Diyoka, director of the influential employers association told Reuters.

Since coming to office in 1994 Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo has tried to implement Western-backed economic reforms aimed at liberalising markets and stamping out the corruption for which Zaire is notorious.

Government spending has been drastically cut, but now faces an added drain as the army prepares to attack the territory occupied by Rwandan-backed Tutsi and other rebels and prevent the chaos spreading further into the country.
"Financing a war is no easy matter and it would be too easy to resort to the printing presses to try and raise enough money," said one Zairean banker.
The army, which earlier this month accused Kengo's government of not doing enough for the war effort, now says it has received the necessary funds. It is not clear where that money has come from.

Substantial reserves of copper and cobalt, as well as gold, diamonds, largely unfelled forests, huge farming and hydro-electricity generating potential mean that Zaire should be one of Africa's richest countries.
Instead it is one of the world's poorest after decades of mismanagement, corruption and sporadic political crises.
As democratic changes swept Africa in 1990, President Mobutu Sese Seko, who seized power in 1965, bowed to the trend and began his own reforms.

But the first four years of the transition, with seven prime ministers, two rounds of army-led looting, and ethnic violence in some of the most economically productive regions, were disastrous for the economy.
Two years of Kengo's government have seen marked macroeconomic improvements, although political pressures on spending have meant 1996 prospects are not looking as bright as in 1995.
Predictions for annual consumer price inflation in 1996 stand at 743 percent. In 1995 it was 382 percent, and in 1994, the year Kengo took office, it reached 6,030 percent.
Growth in 1995 was -0.6 percent, from -3.9 percent in 1994 and -13.5 percent in 1993, according to central bank figures.
Mineral exports have increased and there is renewed interest from foreign investors who turned their backs on Zaire during the early years of chaos.
Current fighting does not immediately threaten the capital, 1600 km (1000 miles) away, or the main economically productive areas of diamond-rich Kasai and the copper and cobalt mines of Shaba.
But the renewed interest could easily be forgotten with the renewed instability.
"In the first half-year of 1996 private foreign investors were looking at bringing $700 million for investments in mining, agriculture and services, with the bulk in the mining sector," said Luboya.
"With the war, it is a matter of wait and see from the point of view of the outside world."
Investors from South Africa, the United States, Canada, Romania and France have all expressed significant interest, Luboya said.
Copper production averaged 3,116 tonnes a month by September 1996, against an average of 2,913 tonnes for the whole of 1995 and 2,553 tonnes in 1994.
Cobalt averaged 421 tonnes a month to September 1996, against 330 tonnes in 1995 and 273 tonnes in 1994.
Diamond exports averaged 1,820 thousand carats to September 1996 against 1,835 thousand carats in 1995 and 1,355 thousand carats in 1994.
Production from Zaire's small reserves of heavy crude oil on the Atlantic coast averaged 29,000 barrels per day in 1996 against 28,000 bpd in 1995 and 25,000 bpd in 1994.

Kengo's government is also trying to increase revenues by decreasing import duties to between five and 30 percent and insisting that payments be made via commercial banks rather than the corruption-riddled customs office.
"1995 and 1996 were years when the seeds of economic recovery were sown and we simply cannot afford to lose that," Luboya said.
($1=81,800 new zaires)
